utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Do the parties wish to address the Chamber with something? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. I'm sorry I wasn't here on Thursday. I was at a -- as Mr. Vanderpuye said, a pre-planned missions, but I, of course, did review the transcripts and review your concerns of the evening prior, and I want to let you know I, of course, share your concerns as I indicated that evening. And, first of all, my remarks to Judge Mindua were absolutely unacceptable and there was -- and without excuse and that will never happen again. Judge Mindua, I am sorry. That will never happen again. I should not let myself get carried away by emotion and you will never see that again. The remarks that led to the problem which I had made in the context of an objection were ill-chosen words when we go back and look at them. They left a strong impression that I was trying to control the witness, and I'm happy in retrospect that Judge Mindua brought that up because I had no idea that I left that impression, but if you look at the words, you're absolutely correct. They were ill-chosen. I did not -- I should not have said that. What I meant to say is, in my view, this witness should be able to leave. And as you know, and as I said that night, we have never had a problem with controlling witnesses or -- or witnesses unavailable. When that happens we work with the Court, with the Defence, and we bring people back, and that will never be our object. That will never happen. It wasn't a problem and it will not be a problem. And my words need to be chosen better, and I regret that they were -- I said what I said, and I'm glad you picked it out because sometimes in the heat of those objections and things, you know, you loose track. There's one thing I hate is lawyers that don't hear themselves, and I hate to have been my own worst enemy in that respect. And if there anything else I can clear up for you about that unfortunate evening, I will. Otherwise, we're ready to go with Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Bear with us for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber has heard what you were addressing to the Chamber. We took note of it and we will consider your position and your submission, and we will come back later to this matter. I would like to raise two other matters at this point in time. We had a notice that the Prosecution didn't file the list of witnesses to be heard this week in time. It came one day too late. And we would like to invite both parties to submit these lists of witnesses including the time which will be needed for examination-in-chief and cross-examination in time, and if it's not possible to file them, we should receive a courtesy copy of such a filing so that we can prepare the hearing in the proper way. So the -- we have another matter. We have to discuss the two exhibits, P01362 and P01363. It's an autopsy report dated 17th of August, 1999, with an associated photograph which were tendered by the Prosecution through Erin Gallagher on the 15th of November 2010 and marked for identification pending translation. The Chamber was informed on the 10th of February that a B/C/S translation of the document, P1362, has now been uploaded. Are there any further submissions regarding the admissibility of this document? This is a question directed to the Defence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning to everybody. I am just looking at these documents, so if we could have a little more time to give an answer to your question, please. Since Witness Gallagher testified quite a while ago, so we would like to remind ourselves of the exhibits and then we can give an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is fine. When can we expect your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow morning at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will come back to that. If there's nothing else, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning. Welcome to the Tribunal and the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you spell your last name for us, for the record?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My family name is Manning, M-a-n-n-i-n-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, you had a chance to testify in the Popovic et al case regarding your years of work here at the OTP in the Srebrenica case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you recently had a chance to review your testimony and the exhibits that came in through you and that you were -- discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, there's quite a long list of material here. Fundamentally the transcripts, it's 65 ter 6764 and 6765, but then I have pages that perhaps we can work out the best way to do this to save time with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The two transcripts will be received as exhibits. The first one 65 ter 06764 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 06764 shall be assigned Exhibit P1818, admitted under seal. 65 ter document 06765 shall be assigned Exhibit P1819. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have, indeed, received a list of associated exhibits admitted through Mr. Manning in the Popovic trial. The first number is 65 ter 06766 and the last one in this list is 65 ter 02201. They will be received as well, but those who don't have a translation yet will be only marked for identification, pending translation. I'm not aware of any of those who don't have a translation. I received an e-mail this morning that two of them have now a translation, but that should be checked again in the whole list. And the Registry will provide the parties and the Chamber with the P numbers of these documents by internal memorandum. Mr. McCloskey go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That accords with Ms. Stewart's records as well. So we'll double-check that. All right. And I'll read a summary now before we get into some questioning. From 1983 to 1998, Mr. Dean Manning worked as a police officer for the Australian Federal Police. In 1998, he came to work in The Hague for the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. For his first four years at the OTP, Mr. Manning was assigned to the Srebrenica investigation as a team investigator. For the last two years of his work for the OTP, Mr. Manning was promoted to the position of investigative team leader for cases involving offences by Bosnian Croats and the case of Slobodan Milosevic. During his work for the Srebrenica team, Mr. Manning was assigned, among other duties, as the co-ordinator of the Srebrenica exhumations programme. As co-ordinator he was responsible for monitoring the ICTY exhumation teams in their work in the field. During the course of this work, he participated in the forensic examination of several mass execution sites and exhumation -- and the exhumation of numerous mass graves associated with the fall of Srebrenica. He worked closely with investigators, archaeologists, anthropologists, forensic pathologists, and others who worked on the exhumations and autopsies of Srebrenica victims and prepared reports compiling and summarising the evidence obtained from the exhumations. He has previous testified before this Tribunal in the Krstic, Slobodan Milosevic case, Blagojevic, and Popovic cases. As part of his work for the Srebrenica team, Mr. Manning, was involved in locating mass graves by working with information from witnesses and examining aerial imagery of disturbed soil provided by the United States government. Mr. Manning reported that the Srebrenica team identified 14 primary mass graves and 22 secondary mass graves, all related to the Srebrenica events. Mr. Manning was personally involved in at least 11 of the exhumations of these sites. In 2001, Mr. Manning oversaw the process of handing over the locations of approximately 20 mass graves to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, who worked in association with the International Commission for Missing Persons, or, as we know it, the ICMP. Mr. Manning headed the small ICTY team that monitored the exhumations conducted by the Bosnian commission. To determine that the mass graves were related to the fall of Srebrenica, Mr. Manning became familiar with the evidence collected by the investigation team, including, statements of survivors and witnesses, and he examined artefacts found within the graves, including identification documents, material related to the Dutch battalion, such as Dutch military rations and Dutch newspapers. From his examination of the aerial imagery of the mass graves, Mr. Manning was able to determine the time-frame in which the mass graves were created. In addition, Mr. Manning reviewed the reports of various experts, including fire-arm examinations of rifle cartridge casings found in and around areas of mass graves and mass executions, analysis of soil and pollen samples from the primary and secondary graves, the analysis of cloth from blindfolds and cloth ligatures found in and around the bodies, as well as artefacts to determine the potential links between primary and secondary graves. Using the reports of various experts, Mr. Manning was able to organise the evidence establishing links between the primary mass graves and secondary mass graves and set them out in a summary form. Mr. Manning prepared reports summarising the most significant findings from the exhumation sites. In his reports from 2000, 2001, and 2003, he set out the exhumation and autopsy process and described the basic process by which material was examined by the experts. In 2003, Mr. Manning reported that the remains of 2570 individuals had been identified, primarily using anthropological criteria and the mass graves exhumed by the ICTY. In 2007, Mr. Manning prepared an updated report that took into account the most current state of knowledge in relation to those graves and, in particular, the number of individuals positively identified by the ICMP through DNA analysis. In this updated 2007 report, Mr. Manning concluded that 4010 individuals exhumed by the ICTY had been identified using DNA analysis. This figure did not include surface remains or mass graves that were exhumed by the Bosnian Commission. In consultation with the experts working in the field, Mr. Manning also reported that the majority of the victims exhumed from ICTY Srebrenica-related mass graves ranged between 20 and 50 years of age. He also reported that the majority of the victims died of gun-shot wounds, although the cause of death was not ascertainable in all cases. Mr. Manning testified that the teams did not recover any item which gave clear indication that the victims were affiliated with any religion -- excuse me, Mr. Manning testified that the teams did not recover any item which gave a clear indication that the victims were affiliated with any religion other than the Islamic faith. During the course of his work, Mr. Manning conducted a physical examination of each artefact and reviewed the associated records, including photographic logs, autopsy reports, and field notes. He reported that a total of 448 blindfolds and 423 ligatures were found in the ICTY graves exhumed during the time-frame of his work. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, can we start the questioning, and I -- for your knowledge and as the Court will recall, we have now heard from all the -- I think most all of the archaeologists and anthropologists. We've heard from Mr. Janc who has updated your work, we've heard from Mr. Ruez, so the Court is very familiar with much of this material. But if we could hit some of the -- some of the high points, I think it will assist the Court, especially as it relates to the ongoing cross-examination. But, first of all, you've been out of the UN for a while now. Can you tell us what your current position is and go back in time for us.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm currently the senior police liaison officer for the Australian Federal Police based in Dubai. I represent the Australian law enforcement efforts in the Middle East, including north Africa. I've held that position for a year. Prior to that, I was the team leader responsible for the Australian Federal Police maritime people smuggling investigations. Prior to that, I was a -- a member of the management training team at the Australian Federal Police college, responsible for senior management training within Australia which was also delivered in China, Indonesia, and Singapore. Immediately prior to that, having left the Tribunal I went to New York where I was employed as a senior investigator with Mr. Folcker investigation of the United Nations Oil for Food programme and the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that update. And from the previous testimony and my summary, we've learned that as the co-ordinator for exhumations you oversaw the hand-over of remaining mass grave locations to the Bosnian commission and ICMP. Can you just explain for that -- explain that just a -- briefly for us. What did that involve?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, prior to the hand-over, the ICTY held responsibility for the exhumation of all the Srebrenica mass-related graves and execution points and were conducting a programme to forensically examine each of those sites with the aim to provide evidence to support the indictment and trials. A decision was made that the responsibility for the examination of those graves and the recovery of the victims would be handed to the Bosnian authorities. I assisted in preparing a memorandum of understanding in which we effectively handed over responsibility for those graves to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons who would be assisted for ICMP and for the first year was monitored by an ICTY team of a forensic anthropologist, archaeologist, and a scene-of-crime officer, and I oversaw the work of that team and the exhumations which were conducted initially by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us was there a difference in focus from the ICTY exhumations and study and the Bosnian Commission exhumations and study?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhumation programme by the ICTY was extremely extensive with the aim of collecting not only the bodies from the mass graves or the execution points but also the evidence, all the physical evidence that we could obtain. The Bosnian Commission, on the other hand, were focussed predominantly on recovering the bodies, taking them from the graves for autopsy with the ultimate aim of identifying bodies and returning the remains to the family. So they were -- much more focussed on the recovery of the bodies. We were focussed on the recovery of the bodies and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And briefly touched in the summary on this topic, but can you explain how it was that when a mass grave was -- was opened, how did you determine whether or not from -- from the contents in the grave at first whether it was related to the Srebrenica events and not some other wartime event or civilian event?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the process was co-ordinated by professional anthropologist, archaeologists, and we were part of that process, but the first order of business on opening a mass grave would be to determine, if we could, any link to Srebrenica or any other crime. The bodies would be initially examined for identification material. We would seek to remove the wallets and the identification documents, and in all the graves that I examined or was part of examining, we would find an identification which either indicated the person had lived or was born in Srebrenica or that their name was on the ICMP missing list or that they there would be an artefact, a Dutch battalion item, or an item indicating that those people were from Srebrenica. And once that was established the rest of the identifications in that material were taken from the grave and examined at the mortuary in more detail to confirm those links.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you were clearly an investigator and part of the investigation team. Did you receive information outside the grave itself that connected any of these graves to the events?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Your Honours, the -- of course, the locations of the graves indicated that they were in the area of Srebrenica and the events that took place. But predominantly we had survivor accounts, people who had been part of the massacres and who had survived, who indicated where the graves were or where the execution points were when they happened. We also relied heavily on aerial imagery provided by the US government which indicated an area, a disturbance in the ground, and a general date and time of that disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Trial Chamber has heard a lot about primary mass graves, execution sites, and secondary. In fact, they have been to many, many of the sites associated with this indictment. They've also heard about the linkages between the primary and the secondary graves from DNA from the bodies from Mr. Janc, but I would like to go back in time before DNA when you were working, did your work involve a -- any investigation into linking the primary mass graves with the secondary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you did that.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the primary mass graves, many of which had been opened up and robbed or the contents removed, indicated that they would be related to a secondary grave. The process of exhuming the bodies identified material in the primary grave that could be linked to the secondary grave. I assisted in the collection and the examination of shell cases, which linked a primary grave to a secondary grave. I assisted Professor Brown in the collection of soil and pollen samples from the mass graves which indicated a link between a primary grave and a secondary grave. I assisted in the examination by Dr. Suzi Maljaars, blindfold and ligatures, cloth blindfolds and ligatures, which again matched primary to secondary graves. And I also assisted in the examination of materials such as green glass and bottle labels which again linked a primary mass grave to several secondary mass graves. The work of the archaeologists and the forensic team was to try and, amongst other things, determine what we could use to link or to exclude links between primary and secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I know this is detailed in your report for each of the graves and that was the subject of your, well, of your reports and some of your prior testimony so I won't go into that, but can you give us just an example, you mentioned shell casings. Can you tell us forensically what that involved, how you were able to match shell casings? In fact, first of all, where did you find shell casings?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you initially examine a mass grave, it's de-mined and made safe. Then the area is metal detected, predominantly to find shell cases or other material. Those shell cases were collected, and as the grave was opened up and the top was scraped off you would find more shell cases and bullets. And you would collect those, photograph them, record where they were in the grave, and as part of the process of examining those shell cases we collected them and conveyed them eventually to the US Department of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Fire-Arms. They examined the shell cases, and I'm not a ballistics expert, but as the shell case is ejected from the weapon, the pin that strikes it and ejects it from the weapon makes a mark on the shell case. That mark, when examined microscopically, is unique to that weapon. So if you take the shell cases and you examine them and you compare those marks, you see that that group of shell cases have the same mark; therefore, they're from the same weapon. They were fired by the same weapon. That examination by Martin Als showed that in the primary grave or on top of the primary grave, amongst the bodies, were shell cases which had been fired from a particular weapon, and a secondary grave, which was sometimes many tens of kilometres away, inside that grave was shell cases which had exactly the same marking. Therefore, they were fired from the same weapon, either into or around the primary grave and then some of them moved to the secondary grave, or perhaps more unbelievable was that the weapon was fired at the primary grave and then fired at the secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say more unbelievable why do you say that in regard to that second comment?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, particularly as the primary graves were established in July of 1995 immediately following or during the executions, and the secondary graves were created several months later, in September and October, opened up, filled with bodies and then sealed. So you had a period of several months between when the shell cases were in the primary grave and would have then been placed in the secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us how or if the investigation was able to establish the time of the executions and creation of the primary graves.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, witness survivor testimony gave us the creation dates or the execution dates and times along with -- perhaps you've heard the evidence of Mr. Erdemovic in relation to two execution points. But also the aerial imagery provided dates and times for the, at least the creation window for the mass graves, and also Professor Richard Wright and a horologist examined wrist-watches from the graves which indicated a time and date of death for those individuals. So a combination of those aspects identified the -- the date and in some instances the time for the creation of those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any, for example, Zvornik brigade engineering documents that sent engineering equipment to any locations that helped in this process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There were vehicle logs which indicated the -- or the work done by machinery in the areas that corresponded to the mass graves. The operators had indicated the time and date, their travel from the base of operations to the mass grave-site, their work on the site, and then return to base. I also believe that there may have been some radio intercepts which indicated date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 2187.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this, I hope, is one of your diagrams exhibiting some of what you have been talking about. And we'll blow this up a bit more in a minute, but do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I do Your Honours. I created this map of primary and secondary graves, and the then established links to those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And because it's so small can you just -- and we'll blow it up in a minute, but can you just tell the Court what is this area north to south that it covers?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It extends from Zeleni Jadar in the south to Branjevo military farm in the north, and out to the Cancari road mass graves. It follows effectively the Drina river, and if you see on the right-hand side of the map was the Serbian territory and on the left-hand side was Bosnia-Herzegovina with Srebrenica and Potocari towards the bottom of the map. From memory, I think it's about 80 kilometres from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we blow up basically the southern half of that that will have Zeleni Jadar. Yeah, that -- you can do it I think one more time. We just want -- we don't need Cancari on there. Yes, that's great. Now we see markings in red marked as primary mass graves. Can you just explain to us the basics of this and how it worked, what it's telling us.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I created the map to show predominantly the mass graves or execution points, and you see those indicated in the map in -- in red, and the green dots indicate secondary graves. And in fact there's a grey point there which is a possible grave. I then labelled the image corresponding to the names we called the graves, and the red lines indicate the links between the graves. It's not necessarily the path that was taken. It's simply that the bodies from the execution at Kravica warehouse were transported to Ravnice grave, which is between 6 and 8 kilometres from the warehouse. Also to the primary grave at Glogova 1 and 2, which is about 8 kilometres from the warehouse. And ultimately from the Glogova graves to the Zeleni Jadar secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I know it's detailed in your report and that you won't be able to remember all the details. We don't need that. But can you give us an example of how you came -- what evidence led you to connect, for example, let's start with the Kravica warehouse to Ravnice, and can you just briefly describe Ravnice? I'm not sure the Court has heard a whole lot about that.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ravnice is an area along a roadway with a steeply sloping side and it was evident that bodies had been dumped down the road way, down the embankment. Initially some soil was taken by a mechanical digger from the side of the road and dumped on the first load of bodies. Thereafter, the bodies were simply dumped down the side of the roadway. They fell down the hill and were caught up in trees and fence lines. I was present at the exhumation of initially Ravnice 1 and a considerable amount of time I spent at Ravnice 2, which is effectively the same grave. It was just labelled 1 and 2. And within that area of grave we found a number of physical artefacts from the warehouse. The warehouse's construction is foam sandwiched between concrete and painted in a particular way. We found pieces of those walls and doors and frames amongst the bodies. We also specifically found a piece of foam lettering which was green and it could be physically matched to the lettering above one of the doors in the warehouse. I think it said, in Bosnian, "otop" [phoen] or "otok," and you could physically see where the piece of foam had been removed or knocked from the building and it had been transported with the bodies to Ravnice mass grave-site. And with Glogova 1 and 2, we found a massive amount of artefacts from the warehouse which showed that the bodies had been collected from the warehouse, driven the 8 kilometres to the very large mass graves, and dumped in those graves. We found those similar artefacts including the walls and parts of the doors in the Zeleni Jadar secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could now go to the north half of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before do you that. I would like to ask a question. Ravnice 1 and 2, and Glogova 1 and 2, are those graves, mass graves, the primary graves in relation to Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Kravica warehouse as an execution point. The bodies were then conveyed to Ravnice, which is on the -- the left-hand side of the main road and also to Glogova 1 and 2. So Ravnice, Glogova 1 and Glogova 2 are primary graves, which received the bodies from Kravica immediately after they were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it that Zeleni Jadar is a secondary grave. Have there been found bodies only from Glogova 1 and 2 or only from 1 -- no, or 2 and not from Ravnice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ravnice 1 and Ravnice, if I can call it one grave, had no evidence that it had been disturbed, so the bodies were pushed down the side of the hill and left. So no bodies that we could see had been removed. Whereas Glogova 1 and 2, in September and October, had been opened up and very heavily dug and all those bodies that they could were removed. So Ravnice 1 was undisturbed; whereas, Glogova 1 and 2 were effectively emptied of much of their contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that regard, the other markings in red Cerska, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje 1 and 2, Sandici, those are marked as primary mass graves only. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. The other graves are primary mass graves and they have not been disturbed. So, if you like, in that image the only graves that have been disturbed are Glogova 1 and 2, and the others were effectively as they were left by the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll -- when we get to the -- some of the secondary images for the secondary graves, we will go over to Glogova because, again, that is something that the Court has not seen much of. It was left out of Mr. Ruez's presentation. All right. If we could now go to the northern part, we're going to -- yeah, we're going to need to take that one down a bit because we need Branjevo and Cancari now -- and the -- you have identified again in red the primary sites of Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, and Branjevo Farm. Is it fair to say that in each of those four cases the archaeologists concluded that they were disturbed primary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- let's just start with Orahovac and tell us what -- what these arrows mean? And just for your knowledge, the Court has been along the road of -- Cancari road and has been up and down this road by the Drina and to the sites of Branjevo Farm, Kozluk, the Dam, and Orahovac. I don't believe we got to the areas of Hodzici or Liplje.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, for Orahovac and the area, and remembering that it's been updated somewhat since, the two Orahovac primary mass graves are very close to each other. They had both been heavily disturbed and the links were made from those primary mass graves to secondary graves; that is, graves that had been created sometime after the primaries again by soil samples, blindfolds and ligatures and shell cases. So Orahovac 1 and 2 were disturbed. The bodies were taken, and at least some of them went to Hodzici road mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during your period, were there -- were all of the known secondary graves at Orahovac fully exhumed and examined?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The majority of the Hodzici road graves were examined. I believe that number 1 we suspected had not been used. It was examined by the Bosnian commission and found to contain bodies, and I believe there may have been a additional grave on Hodzici road examined by the Bosnian commission. But we worked through the Hodzici road mass graves. We had exhumed 3, 4, and 5 during our exhumations period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go next to the dam. Tell us a bit about that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The mass grave at the dam near Petkovci had been built into the stone wall of the dam, and when it had -- when it was examined it was very thoroughly emptied and robbed of the contents. We were able to examine the Liplje mass graves and match the rocks and the matrix of that -- of those secondary graves to the primary grave at the dam, so the -- some of the bodies taken from the dam were placed in the Liplje mass graves, secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know this is identified in -- thoroughly in your reports, but besides the rocks from this constructed dam, do you remember any other connections like you've talked about before?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd have to check the report, but the soil and pollen samples from the dam site matched those at the -- at the Liplje site as well as the particular large boulders which formed the part of the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Kozluk, you've connected Kozluk down, if we see from the arrows to two sites in your time along the Cancari road. How did that work?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Kozluk mass grave had been heavily disturbed. The bodies taken from that grave. When we examined the Cancari road graves, the secondary graves, we saw that there were in the graves many fragments of green glass, broken bottles, including bottle labels. Those same labels were at the Kozluk site which is actually a rubbish dump, and predominantly dumped there were broken glass bottles from the Vitinka bottling factory, which was nearby. So the bodies, when they were executed, lay amongst the green glass, that green glass was picked up, taken to Cancari road where it was not otherwise present, and dumped within the secondary graves. We also had shell cases which matched. Again, that examination showed that the same weapon was at the primary grave and in the secondary grave. And cloth blindfolds and ligatures from the Kozluk mass grave were the same -- were indistinguishable from the ones in the secondary grave. So you had a great number of matches that showed that the Kozluk grave, the contents had been placed into at least some of the Cancari road graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And finally we have the Branjevo Farm and we see that there's an arrow to least one site in that area of Cancari road. Can you just update us on those results.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The primary mass grave at Branjevo Military Farm had been extensively robbed. And we located soil and pollen samples which matched the site at Branjevo Military Farm within the secondary graves at the other end of the Cancari road, so the soil and pollen were foreign to that area. And we also had blindfolds predominantly which were the same at the Branjevo farm site on the bodies that had been left and the same as -- on the bodies that were found in the Cancari mass grave, secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now you've explained briefly how the dates of the primary mass graves and executions were determined from the various parts of evidence. How were you able to determine if -- if you were, the dates of creation of the secondary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, specifically, the aerial imagery provided the location and the creation date range for those secondary graves. Most of them were in very remote areas and would have been very difficult to find without those images. But they showed a date when the soil had not been disturbed and a date when the soil had been disturbed. So within that window was when the secondary graves were created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you given aerial images for all the primary graves on this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: For the primary graves and for the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you make a careful analysis of the dates and provide those materials in your prior testimony and in your report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not going to go through all that again, of course, but I would like to use one or two examples, especially let's start with Glogova, because that the Court has not seen, I don't believe, aerial imagery in detail on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 1046.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about Glogova and -- you've mentioned I think before that there was a couple of graves there. How does a -- what do you mean when you say a couple of pits or graves in the Glogova area?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The Glogova primary mass graves were about 8 kilometres from Kravica. You followed a dirt road, and on the left and right-hand side of the dirt road were very large mass graves, and again they had been disturbed. So the graves were created by machinery and that was clear, and then had been opened up and very, very heavily dug and re-dug and then flattened out, and you can see that not only on the aerial image but also I could see that as a layman in the soil which is pointed out to me by the archaeologist. You can see the disturbance in the soil and the teeth marks and wheel marks of the machines that dug the grave and then re-dug the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at this particular exhibit it says Tatar-Bratunac. Is that the Glogova grave as you know it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the image is not very good, but if you see the GL-1 mark on those images I placed those mark there on top of the image. It shows in July of 1995 an extensive area to the right of the roadway which is in the middle that had been disturbed. And then on the right hand pane in October, you can see that it has been again disturbed from what was like in July, so it was re-dug sometime prior to and continuing on the 20th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say you put in the yellow markings. How about the markings in white blocks, the grave exhumation, the dates, conclusion of burial site, conclusion of excavator, conclusion of trench, who put -- can you remind us who put that information on this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was provided by the providers of the image, the US government. So effectively, all the white details are from them. They called it Tatar-Bratunac area. We knew it as Glogova, so we called the grave Glogova 1 and I labelled it GL-1. The rest is produced by the US government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that disturbance of 27 of July and 20 October. We have not gone into the dates prior to Srebrenica or around Srebrenica, but was there similar aerial photography that showed this area with no disturbance?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. And I would have to check the dates. But there was imagery that showed that area undisturbed so that we knew that prior to at least the 27th of July on this image, there was an image that showed it was a bare field with some damaged houses and then we see the grave has been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 1047, remembering that this image is of 27 July and 20 October. Okay. Now we see an image of 30 October. Does this have anything to do with the last image, the location of the last image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a larger view of the same area. If you see starting at the bottom middle and moving up to the right a roadway, that divides, if you like, Glogova 1 from Glogova 2. Glogova 1 is the grave that was shown in the previous image. You can see very clearly that there is a large amount of earth being moved and pushed right up against the road, right up against the houses, and in that image you can also see that Glogova 2 has been opened up and there is a very large amount of digging happening. You can see the tire tracks in this image, and you can see that that mass grave has been opened up and the other mass grave has also been opened up and looks to me as if it's been sealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you take the pen - maybe you'll get some help with that - and circle what tire tracks you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, in this image, remembering that I'm not an expert in aerial imagery, but I can see it and I know what was on the ground. If you look at Glogova 2, you can see parallel lines on that image. I know them to be vehicle tracks. And if you look on the GL-1 image, you can see again parallel lines, and even in the other part of that image you can see parallel lines which have been displayed out where the machines have been pushing the soil. And again from this image, I can match it to what I saw in the soil and in the exhumation which showed those marks and the tracks of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would offer this -- this image with the three circles that he's drawn around the parallel lines into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if the witness could put number 1 and number 2 and number 3 next to the three circles in the -- in the order that you made these circles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This marked aerial image will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map shall be assigned Exhibit P1820. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we go to 65 ter 1089. Now, I'll recall that you mentioned that -- in -- that the Zeleni Jadar secondary graves were related or came from Glogova, based on your analysis. And can you tell us -- well, we see again an aerial image marked as Zeleni Jadar. Does -- you recall -- do you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The image is poor quality and I hope you will be able to see a better version. But it's a split image. So the image on the left was provided or taken on the 24th of August, 1995, and the one on the right is exactly the same area, except on the 2nd of October. If you see that band running across the middle of the image, there is a river, a small river in that area, and a roadway. Now between the roadway and the river, in August, there's no sign of disturbance. And in October you can see a trench, a grave was dug. I've visited that area and walked through that area and examined it with Professor Wright, and there was a pit dug there, and in fact we examined it and found that the majority of the bodies had removed from that grave. Therefore, meaning that there was a third level or a tertiary grave somewhere. But this image effectively shows the creation window of dates for that secondary mass grave which was created some several months after the related primary graves were created of Glogova 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you went there with Professor Wright and that there there was a pit there. Can you explain that? Was there a pit there when you got there or was that something that was determined?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The -- the hole had been filled in and Professor Wright, an archaeologist, examined it. He concluded that there had been a hole there which had been filled in and there were clear signs of disturbance. He also indicated that there were scattered human remains throughout that area and that those human remains were from more than one individual. He concluded that had it -- had been a mass grave that had been dug up and then filled back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now let's go to 1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This again -- what is this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's effectively the same area, the river running through the middle. The grave on the bottom. If you see those two -- two labels, ZJ-2, I placed those on that image. On 20th of October, 1995, you can see the mass grave had been created, and in the other image on the 23rd of October you could see that it's been effectively sealed, and I've seen a better quality image than this. So you can see the grave opened or built on the 20th of October 1995, and on the right hand pane the grave closed in and finished. And that was reflected all along Zeleni Jadar where you saw graves 1, 2, 6, or 7, created, dug and then filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your previous testimony have you had photographs like this of the majority, if not all, of the Zeleni Jadar graves so that this process can be seen?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact for the Zeleni Jadar 5 grave we used the same sort of image to locate it. And for the Zeleni Jadar 6 grave, I stood at the grave with the archaeologists with that image, and that's how we found the mass grave against the roadway in a field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So I think the details of the other secondary graves and the aerial images that go along with them are all in your report or in your prior testimony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go back to 65 ter 2187. And that's the linkage map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I just want it to be the backdrop of this next question which was the subject matter of some of your testimony last time and has been the subject matter of this case. Has, in your experience as an investigator, was there any evidence that any battle casualties from the column's departure from Susnjari on through Baljkovica to Nezuk, was there any evidence that any of those battle casualties or surface remains or unknown deaths were placed in any of the mass graves? And let's start with Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could do what we did last time, just blow up Glogova so they can picture where that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my immediate answer is no. There wasn't evidence of battle casualties within any of the graves that are depicted on this map. I must admit, I was not involved in Sandici so I can't say for Sandici. In -- in person. But particularly for Glogova 1 and 2, there were bodies within the graves which indicated that they had been executed at the Kravica warehouse. There wasn't -- there wasn't evidence that they had been collected elsewhere. There wasn't a difference in the bodies that would have shown that they were collected from this site, this site, this site, and dumped. They were all consistent and they were consistently surrounded by pieces of the warehouse. Glogova 1 and 2 are very large graves and the aerial images indicate that they were open for some time, and I am aware that one of the graves - I think it's grave L - was created after or at the end of the creation of Glogova 1 and 2. That grave contained 12 individuals who had been bound and shot in the head and some in the chest, and they were placed at the edge of the Glogova 2 mass grave. But, again, there was not, to my discussions with the experts and my examinations of the mass graves, indications that bodies from a battle had been placed in those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it possible that if there had been some Muslims that had died while crossing the asphalt road between Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Bratunac that those bodies could have been picked up and put in Glogova without leaving a significant archaeological trace?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. Again I didn't see that and I'm not an archaeologist but that's possible. But given the nature of the site and the remains, I would suggest if that happened it would be very few bodies amongst the many bodies that were in those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the northern site, the northern sites, if -- like you did before. Thank you. Now, again, any evidence that there were any battle casualties put in the Orahovac primary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: None, Your Honours. Apart from the location of the Orahovac grave which is, as I understand it, not immediately near the battles, the individuals within the graves many of them were blindfolded. We have a witness account of the -- of the execution of the blindfolding from the school nearby and the individuals being taken to the mass graves. We found a hundred or more blindfolds at that site which were not collected. We found blindfolds at the school where the witness described being blindfolded, and we found again the bodies within both those graves indicating that they had been executed in situ at that site and then buried there. There was not an indication that they had been collected elsewhere and taken to that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, Petkovci is a remote location. There was evidence from numerous shell cases at the site that there had been an execution in that area, but remembering that there were very few body parts at that grave. In the related Liplje grave, there was no indication that the individuals had been killed in battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall whether there were survivors that talked about that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: And again, I believe, there are two survivors, and you may have heard from both of them, that described the execution. The transportation to the dam site, the lining up and the gunning that -- the shooting down of those individuals at that site. They didn't describe a battle. They were prisoners and they were executed at that site and buried at that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Kozluk, remembering that it's in the middle of a rubbish dump. It's a field of -- of tons of broken glass next to the Drina river. There's evidence that the individuals were shot there. They were then -- they fell onto the ground, the original surface, and then they were covered with soil. We found bodies with bullet-holes through the bodies and in the ground beneath them bullets. We found individuals who were bound and blindfolded, and we found an individual, to my recollection, who had clearly been shot and crawled away from the edge of the grave and was buried where he lay with his hand grasping a bush. It was clear that those individuals were executed at that site and that they weren't battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly, Branjevo military or Branjevo farm?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours may have heard the testimony of Mr. Erdemovic who describes the execution of those individuals in the field at Branjevo farm. I believe we also have a survivor from that execution. And again, within that primary mass grave, and I indicate I wasn't present for the exhumation of that grave, but I was for the related graves, there was no indication that those bodies were from battle. That they had been killed in battle. Rather, that they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned briefly, and I mentioned in the summary, your conclusions of some numbers of blindfolds and ligatures. Can you briefly explain to the Court how you made your determination whether something was a blindfold and ligature for your summary report on that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhumation who process had gone on for several years, so you had people who worked in the field, people who worked in the mortuary, and they changed over the years. A blindfold or a ligature might be seen on a body in the mass grave, and by the time it was transported to the mortuary had fallen off the head or the wrists or, indeed, the body had fallen apart. So you had a situation where the count of blindfolds at the grave was different to the count of blindfolds or ligatures at the mortuary. I examined every single record that related to those blindfolds and ligatures. I went to the -- I was present at most of the exhumations, but I also went to the written records, the photographs at the grave-site, the reports by the archaeologists and anthropologists and the photographs and reports at the mortuary. I then physically examined each of those items, and if I could show that there was a blindfold on the head or near the face of an individual, if I could prove that it was around a cloth with hair in the knot of the blindfold, I would count it as a blindfold. If, on the other hand, they had made a mistake and not photographed that item and I couldn't definitively prove that it was a blindfold or a ligature, I would discount it. I would not count it in my total. So I was very conservative in my examination of the blindfolds and ligatures, and I had a trial, if you like, to prove that that blindfold was indeed on that body in that grave when it was located. And if I couldn't find that written or photographic proof, I put that blindfold aside and said there was only 448 instead of a great many more. An example is the blindfolds at Grbvaci school and at the Orahovac-Lazete mass graves. I've seen photographs of those blindfolds and I've spoken to the investigators who saw them, but because I didn't have them and I couldn't prove that they had been found on the bodies, I discounted those, I think, 207 blindfolds. So it is a very conservative number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I have a number of questions. Maybe I will start with the last one. In your testimony just now you have said something about some dying in battle or not in battle. How do you determine whether a person was killed -- was killed in battle or not in battle? How can you distinguish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I must advise you I'm not an archaeologist or an anthropologist or a pathologist. But where we saw clear evidence that the person had been shot at an execution point, that, to me, is evidence that they were not killed in battle. An individual at the Kozluk mass grave-site had their wrists bounds behind their back and they were shot and you can see that that body had fallen forward on the ground and then were buried in that position. So clearly, to me, those individuals were executed. The other individuals within that grave who perhaps did not have a blindfold or a ligature didn't show any difference. They didn't show that they had been blown up by a mine and scooped up by a machine and dumped into the grave. Or that their arms and legs had been held and they'd been thrown into the grave. If you saw casualties picked up from a battlefield, you would expect to see that sort of information reflected in the graves, and it wasn't. The mass graves, the execution points, contained bodies and individuals that indicated that they had been executed, not that they had been fighting and had been shot in -- in 20 different locations through the Bosnian country-side and then collected up. If that happened with a machine, I would expect to see the machine scoop the body up and dump it in a truck. So you would have soil from that location. You would have soil from that location, et cetera. We didn't see that. We saw the bodies either executed there or dumped into the mass graves, say at Glogova, and that consistency and the presence of blindfolds, the presence of ligatures, the witness testimony, and the testimony of the executioners indicate to me that they weren't battle casualties, that they were, in fact, prisoners who had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So if somebody was shot in battle and dumped in the grave, they have not been executed. You can tell that they have not been executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I'm conscious that I'm not an archaeologist, or a pathologist, if, for instance, at Kozluk which is in a remote location where there is no battle, there is no fighting going on there. If someone had brought a body from elsewhere to that site, I would expect to see a difference in that group of bodies. If they brought one body, we wouldn't know that that person was not executed. If they brought ten bodies, you would expect to see when those bodies were collected that a -- say they collected them with a machine. You would expect the machine to scoop up those ten bodies and dump them in a truck, so they would have a layer of soil which would be different to Kozluk. It wouldn't -- certainly wouldn't be the same. If they'd picked those bodies up and thrown them in the back of a truck and then driven them to Kozluk and then dumped, you would see a tangle of ten bodies or a hundred bodies in that area of the grave. You would see that they had been dumped in the grave, or you would see that they had been thrown into the grave. We didn't see that. At Kozluk we saw them executed and falling where they were shot. Does that assist, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. My next question is in relation to your testimony at page 25, lines 8 to 10, where you state: "From this imagery, I can match it to what I saw in the soil and in the exhumation which showed those marks and the tracks of the vehicles." How soon after the exhumations did you have an opportunity to visit the sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for Glogova 1 and 2, those mass graves were created in July of 1995 and disturbed in October, September/October. I was present at the opening of both those graves, which would be four years later. So the graves had been created then covered up. I came in with the archaeologists who then painstakingly removed the soil, and in the soil I could see those tracks. So from when they were initially buried to when I saw them would be in the region of four years -- three to four years continuing over a -- I think a two-year period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. How many mass graves were you personally involved with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Srebrenica -- Srebrenica mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least 11 where I had a significant involvement, where I was either the one who -- who found the grave with the assistance of the imagery or I was present when it was opened or I was present for several weeks, and the majority of the other graves which hadn't been exhumed by the time I had arrived, I visited. So 11 mass graves I had a significant involvement with, and the majority of the others I had visited or I had gone to after they had been exhumed or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: One last question, if you will excuse me. How did you exactly know where these graves were located for you to start the process of exhumations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in some instances we had the witnesses who told us, the survivors who told us where they were. By the majority of times, I held an image in my hands from the US government and we would go to that site, and you see, for instance, the Glogova road, you would see that road. So I would stand there with the image and we would say, Right, we think it's there. It matches to being there. The archaeologists would then examine the area, and then they would scrape the soil from the area. And very often you would see the shape of the grave. You would see the outline of the hole that was dug, and when you dig a hole and fill it in, you can see that, and also the fluids would leak from the bodies and form a dark stain in the soil, and we would see that. But to give you an idea, even with the aerial imagery, standing from here to the -- to the next table away, we could sometimes not find that grave. In one instance we had the image, we had a tree where we thought the grave was near, we had the road and we missed it, and it took us 24 hours of digging to find the edge of the grave. And as soon as we saw the soil with the discolouration, as soon as we saw shoes and clothing we knew we'd found the edge of the grave. We took the surface off and you could see the grave and the staining from the bodies, and then we would start digging that grave. So predominantly looking at the aerial imagery and showing that imagery against the ground and what it related to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is the time for our first break. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Before the cross-examination, I wanted to have some clarification from you. You played an important role in the investigation because, if I look at today's transcript, page 35, line 16 -- lines 16 and 17, you state that you were among the first ones to find, to discover, the mass graves. My question would be as follows. Have you found bodies on the surface of the mass graves as well? This is what I like to know. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, if I can just point out, we found the mass graves, as in we located them. But, effectively, in many cases we knew where they were beforehand. We knew that they were in that location. So when I say "we found them," it was the process of saying that area is a mass grave, and then we confirmed that that was a mass grave. But as to surface remains, at the majority of the mass graves we did not find surface remains. The individuals were well-buried underneath the soil, several metres of soil. In Kozluk, when I first visited the site, there were human remain remains that were visible from the soil. There was a leg and an arm and another leg sticking out of the soil, and I believe the reason was that that area had been eroded, that the body had appeared from rain. And underneath that was several hundred bodies. At Orahovac 1, there was a single body which was on the surface, and it became evident that that body had been pushed against a fence by the digging machine that had dug up the grave. You could see the tracks of the machine pushed the body and the soil out of the grave and onto the surface. And we found that when we started examining the body -- the mass grave. But, in the majority of graves, except Ravnice, the bodies were well buried. In Ravnice, the majority of the bodies had been thrown down the embankment. So they were open to the elements and they were completely skeletonised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. What would be your idea of the proportion? What proportion would there be of remains at the surface and remains in the mass graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozluk, we saw maybe three body parts and within that grave there were at least 350 bodies. At Orahovac there was one single body and there was several hundred within the mass grave. So in the mass graves we saw very view surface remains, 1, maybe 2 per cent, less than 1 per cent, except for Ravnice which was all surface remains in that they had been pushed down the hill-side and were on the surface. I'm not sure if that is -- answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'll keep it at this for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There must be a technical problem. We don't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that they can't hear the accused despite the microphone being on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please try to use the other microphone for a moment? There seems to be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can you hear me now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we received interpretation, that means the interpreters understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Peace unto this house and may this day in court -- may God's will be done in these proceedings and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. I welcome Mr. Manning and I would appreciate his assistance in uncovering the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me start, Mr. Manning, from some of the points that were raised during the examination-in-chief. Judge Mindua has just asked you about surface remains. His question was whether it was easier to find bodies that were on the surface or in the ground. On page 37 of the transcript, your answer was that you found one body in Orahovac and three in Kozluk so a total of four individuals next to the mass graves. Are you referring only to the mass graves at Orahovac and Kozluk, were you referring to only those in this answer of yours or did you have in mind the whole of the 11 mass graves that you uncovered?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was referring to all the ICTY mass graves in that they were graves that were dug into the soil and the bodies were placed into them. The reason there were surface remains from both those graves that I mentioned was a part of that burial process. I was not discussing remains that may have been located in areas outside the mass graves. I'm only speaking about the mass graves that the ICTY located, more than 11 mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many surface remains you found from among these 11 mass graves that were investigated by the ICTY? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to 11 mass graves, but in also the other 44, the ones I've mentioned, three body parts at Kozluk and one individual on the surface at Orahovac. I don't recall other surface remains amongst the mass graves. The mass graves had been dug and sealed, and in those that had been disturbed had been re-dug and re-sealed so that the remains were not laying on the surface but were under the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise if I am repeating the question. But can you tell us the exact number of surface remains you found in all of the 55 graves that were located without going into any extensive explanation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Speaking about the ICTY graves, and I think when we left, we were at the point of 44 mass graves, I would say that surface remains were located at two of those graves. One individual at Orahovac. And parts of three, perhaps, individuals at Kozluk. No more. That I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can I therefore conclude that you found a total of four bodies on the surface close to the mass graves that you investigated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, and Mr. Tolimir, I'm trying to be accurate. I can say one body, certainly at Orahovac. And parts of what I believe to be three bodies at Glogova. And I say "believed" because we didn't remove those bodies when we first saw them. We exhumed Glogova -- sorry, Kozluk as a mass grave, so those remains that were sticking out of the ground were probably later identified as complete bodies. But I can only say that there were human remains visible on the surface of Kozluk which looked like three individuals. And when we came back several months later to conduct the exhumation, that's when the entire mass grave was exhumed and those body parts were collected as part of that exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. In addition to the locations you describe just now, namely, Kozluk and Orahovac where you found one body at Kozluk and three body parts at Glogova, was there any other grave or any other location where you found surface remains? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware that the Bosnian commission found another, I believe from memory, 12 bodies on the surface at Kozluk nearby the mass graves. I wasn't part of that process. And I believe that collections of surface remains were made by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and the ICMP. The ICTY did not collect body parts or surface remains but concentrated on identified or located mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell us where the 12 bodies that were found on the surface were ultimately located and are they numbered among all the others killed at Glogova? You said that where they were killed that's where their bodies fell. Where were they ultimately buried, these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to Kozluk. We exhumed the Kozluk mass grave. We removed all the bodies from the -- from the mass grave itself, and I'm not talking about Glogova. We -- or I was aware that there were other areas of disturbance around the mass grave that you could see from the images. Myself and other investigators spoke to Mr. Murat Hutic from the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I indicated to him that we did not find surface remains but that he could perhaps look wider from the mass grave, and he subsequently did so. He found a number of bodies, and I would -- I would be guessing to say several hundred metres from the primary mass grave that we'd exhumed but certainly in the area. But I wasn't involved in that process. I believe he found the bodies because we had told him that there were other tyre tracks and disturbances in the area, and he searched the area and found those bodies. As to where they are now, they would have been part of the DNA process undertaken by ICMP and the Bosnian Commission and, hopefully, they've been returned to the families, but I believe that they have been linked through DNA to the Srebrenica massacres. I believe it's 12, but I would have to check the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Was it easier to find bodies that were buried several metres into the ground, as you said, or was it easier to recover the surface remains? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been easier to recover the surface remains. Digging a mass grave is a very lengthy and expensive process. That was not our focus. The collection of surface remains was not our focus. But it is easier to pick up surface remains but many of the surface remains would have been in areas that were inaccessible that perhaps were in minefields, and spread out over many square kilometres. We concentrated on mass graves that we knew existed, particularly those that were connected to execution points, but our focus was not to collect surface remains. Had we found them we would have either collected them or we would have advised the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. An example is Ravnice. Surface remains were located I think by the SFOR troops. They pointed them out to us. We examined the site and because of the -- the high number, we exhumed that grave. As I say, we concentrated on mass graves, not on surface remain, which were not present at our mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell us how many bodies were found on the surface in Ravnice after you were referred to that location by the SFOR, as you said? Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd have to check my report. And I don't recall. I think it was about 140, 150, but because the bodies were broken up, that count would be best obtained from the DNA analysis of those remains because the bodies broke up. From my recollection I think 150, but that number would have been better determined since I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you indicate a location that was closest to Ravnice where the surface remains were found?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not sure that I understood the question. The Ravnice grave-site, and we called it that for -- for ease of reference, was in the area of Ravnice, it was on a dirt track to the left of the main road running past the Kravica warehouse, and it stretched for several hundred metres along the side of the road. It wasn't in a village. It was on a roadway between, I think, Hodzici in the Ravnice area. It was very close to the Kravica warehouse. From memory, you could -- you could see the warehouse from an area near the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Tell us, since we've now established that this is close to Kravica and one was able to see the Kravica warehouse, can you tell us what the cause of death of the individuals found on the surface was found to be? Was it the result of fighting or execution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'd have to check my report for the specific numbers. I believe the majority had been killed by gun-shot injury. There was also blast injury as in grenades injuries. I believe we found some evidence of -- of charring on the bodies. And that has to be linked to the large number of artefacts from the Kravica warehouse which surrounded those bodies. If you're asking me as to the cause of death, those bodies were killed whilst in the Kravica warehouse and their bodies were then dumped at Ravnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you referring to the surface remains found at Ravnice or the remains found in a grave there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ravnice, if that's a road, and that's an embankment running down to a small stream, trucks had driven along that road and dumped the bodies at an angle down the -- the embankment. At this end, they had been covered by soil, a small mechanical scoop of soil. The rest of the bodies had simply been pushed over the edge. To refer to them as surface remains I believe would indicate that they were spread over an area where they'd been killed. These were dumped in an area. They were pushed over the edge and there was a collection of bodies, most of which hadn't been covered with soil. To my definition, that's a grave, an open grave. But you -- if I may, you should see the Ravnice site as a grave rather than a collection of surface remains. The bodies were pushed together, they were poured out of a truck, and they'd collected against trees and against fence lines. The skulls in many cases had fallen off and rolled down the hill, and the bodies, whilst clothed, were skeletons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, at a later date, through the exhumation and DNA analysis, did you establish that the bodies had their skulls found in the primary grave at Kravica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. From my recollection, there was no connection from the Ravnice to the Glogova mass graves. And when I refer to the skulls falling off and rolling away, they moved 20 metres from the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
