utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't mentioning Glogova, from what I remember. My question was: Did you find these bodies together with the other bodies of those killed at Kravica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The people, the men and boys were killed at Kravica warehouse, they were loaded onto trucks, and they were transported to Ravnice along with parts of the warehouse, and those bodies were not then removed. And the rest of the bodies were picked up in trucks and driven to Glogova 1 and 2, where they were dumped. So Ravnice, once the bodies were dumped there, was left alone, until we exhumed it. The bodies in Glogova 1 and 2, from the warehouse, were initially buried and then unburied and taken to the secondary graves. So the bodies in Ravnice would not have been transported to Glogova. They would, however, have been taken from the Kravica warehouse which was not a mass grave but an execution point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, what I'm not clear on is why we have this misunderstanding. You were just mentioning the bodies in Ravnice. What I'm asking you is: The surface remains at Ravnice, were they bodies that were exhumed or were they on the surface?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the bodies, some of the bodies at Ravnice were covered by soil, intentionally covered by soil. We came and we took the soil off and we recovered the bodies. The rest of the bodies had not been covered by soil, so we recovered those bodies by removing the soil that washed onto them over the years, by removing the bushes and the trees and finding the body parts that had fallen down the hill. So we say we exhumed that mass grave, even though a proportion of that mass grave was open to the air. Does that -- I'm trying to explain that the Ravnice grave was a dumping ground for bodies from the Kravica warehouse. Part of it was covered with soil, but the rest of it was simply a dumping ground where tens of bodies were pushed over the side of the ledge, of the embankment, and collected down the hill-side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the bodies were pushed downhill, were they in a grave or on the surface? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a mass grave. A mass grave of 150 people where the bodies are touching is a grave, as far as I'm concerned. And I'm not sure if I -- I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you received at least three times the exact ... received at least three times the exact description of the understanding and the observations of the witness of this site, where bodies were found. Some under soil, some uncovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Actually, I just need a clarification. When is a place a grave? When it has been dug up and bodies -- or bodies put in it, or any place where you find a body becomes a grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so. But when we're talking about mass graves, and in this instance multiple bodies, if you look at the Cerska grave, the men were shot by the side of the road and then they fell and they simply took soil from the side of the road and covered them up. That's clearly a grave. Even though they weren't dug, a hole was not dug and they weren't put in the hole, they were covered by soil. For the Ravnice grave, I believe it is a mass grave, in that part of the bodies were covered by soil. A hole wasn't dug. The bodies were pushed down the slope and some of them were covered by soil. The rest weren't. But that collection of bodies is the same event, so it's the same group of bodies, and I think that could you have a situation where you put 500 bodies in a pile and did not cover them up, and I - and I'm not an expert anthropologist or archaeologist - I would still describe that as a grave, as a collection of bodies in one spot. Had none of the bodies at Ravnice been covered by soil, perhaps we would have called it something different. But it was a -- it was a spot where a significant number of bodies were dumped in the one location, some of them were covered with soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Manning, the grave at Ravnice, is it considered by you or the OTP as a grave, a grave-site, or as a location of surface remains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's considered by the ICTY, the OTP, as a grave-site, and it's referred to as an exhumed mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So the OTP does not treat it as a location of surface remains. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The OTP treats it as a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't need a lot of time to find surface remains, and since before the discovery of the mass graves you talked to many witnesses who could tell you about them, please tell us why surface locations were not investigated, locations that witnesses talked about?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: When I came to the Tribunal, the Tribunal had already established the exhumations team with the intention of exhuming mass graves. The surface remains, at that time and continuing, were being collected by the Bosnian commission. And we're talking about several hundred square kilometres where bodies were located. The Tribunal made a decision to exhume mass graves, particularly where those mass graves were linked to a witness account of an execution. We had Mr. Erdemovic saying he executed hundreds and hundreds of men at the Branjevo Military Farm and that there was a mass grave there. As part of the investigation of that incident, and Mr. Erdemovic's story, we exhumed the mass grave. We were collecting evidence to support or to -- or to prove that the offence didn't happen or that the offence happened in a certain way. And we're talking about genocide where men and boys were blindfolded and tied up and shot, and the evidence of that was in those mass graves. The collection of surface remains was carried out by other agencies. I can only say that the ICTY made a decision to exhume the mass graves and to investigate the killing of those men and boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you consider every murder genocide or only the murders that you talked about where you found a certain number of binds and blindfolds and the number which is 880 of which 448 were for the head and the rest for the hands? Did these same people have blindfolds as well as -- and were their hands tied at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: To answer your question in relation to genocide, no. Every murder is clearly not a genocide. The finding of a genocide was made by one of the Courts here at the Tribunal, and that was the investigation that we were part of. Yes, some of the individuals were blindfolded and were tied. I would have to check my report. Some individuals not only blindfolded but had their hands tied behind their backs. Some had their hands tied behind their backs. Some had blindfolds but were not bound. I think two individuals had their legs tied. In the Cerska grave, I think 31 out of 33 had their wrist wrists tied -- sorry. At Cerska I think it was up to 100 out of the 150. But I would have to check my reports for specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But since you're an investigator and since it's up for the Court to decide what's genocide and what's not, is it appropriate for you as an investigator to decide what's genocide and what isn't?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure I quite understand the question. I understood that in several verdicts a genocide charge for Srebrenica has been upheld. But I, as an investigator, investigated an allegation of a genocide, an allegation of mass killings, an allegations of crimes against humanity and of war crimes. That was the investigation I was part of. Since that time, the events of Srebrenica have been defined by a court, several courts as genocide. I don't claim to make that assertion. I was investigating a genocide, but I don't claim that I classify as a genocide outside the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Now you mentioned crimes against humanity and against peace. During your work and during your investigations, as you said, you mentioned all the crime, did you find any crimes against peace? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you heard in the UN Charter that there is something called a crime against peace? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I -- I'm going to have to say no. I'm not quite aware of an offence that's a crime against peace. I'm aware of crimes against the peace, of crimes which relate to disorder. But, I'm sorry, I'm missing the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't understand what I'm trying to say, you did not investigate crimes against peace in Srebrenica and in the other areas where you were engaged as an investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It -- Your Honours, if you mean offences committed against other people, not the Srebrenica victims, do you mean offences committed by the Muslims of Bosnia or the Croats of Bosnia? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. I have no right to say what I think. I only have a right to ask the my questions, and if you can, you will answer them. My question, the following one, is this: Is it the same people who are responsible both for peace and for war?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I -- I don't think I can answer that. I investigated allegations specifically related to Srebrenica and the killing of men and boys. I also assisted other teams in the investigation of offences where Serbs were victims, particularly one team I assisted in their investigation of, I believe, Naser Oric. But I can't answer your question as to are the same people responsible for peace and for war. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us this: In the former Yugoslavia where you investigated, among others, Srebrenica, did Yugoslavia disintegrate as a result of the will of the people living in it and who waged war or was this conceived by forces outside the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I simply can't answer that question. My opinion as to how the war started or who was involved, is simply that. I'm not a historian. I'm sorry, I can't answer. If you want my opinions as a layperson I can give them, but I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not what I want. I merely wanted to know what you investigated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at D151 in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is confidential exhibit should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, please look when this document was drafted. In paragraph 1 it says: "On 20 July 1996, an unknown person came," and we will not say his name, "to the commission for gathering facts on war crimes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was no question yet, I think. What is your question, Mr. Tolimir? It is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Manning, was this witness heard before you started investigating crimes because he was heard on the 20th of July 1996? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this particular statement. I would have to check whether I know the individual. I'm sorry, I haven't seen that statement before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he is going to be asked about this individual and this statement, he should be allowed to read the entire statement because I think it becomes very clear from the statement. So if -- if he's interested in that, I think he should be allowed to read it to help refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, if Mr. Tolimir is continuing to put questions in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked whether Mr. Manning started his investigations before the 20th of July, 1996. He doesn't need to read the statement for that. Can he answer my question of whether he started his investigations before the 20th of July, 1996? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not. Because I joined the Tribunal in August of 1998, and I continued thereafter the work of the Srebrenica team. But from my knowledge of the team, I know that the investigation of the Srebrenica genocide started at the time the offences were occurring and immediately thereafter. Mr. Ruez was involved in the investigation from July of 1995, and certainly from the end of that year, when he was able to access the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But for myself, I didn't start investigating this offence until August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. So we can say that after this statement was given you started working as an investigator. Should you be familiar with this statement as an investigator, as this is a statement which talks about bodies and where these bodies can be found? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now that he has referred to the statement and he's referred to material in it that's probably on, let's hope, on the next page or two, it would be appropriate if the witness could be allowed to read the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read the first page now, in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If you mean I can read it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Let's look at page 2. Could we look at the third paragraph which is relevant. Line 7 in paragraph 3, that is line 4, I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3, paragraph 4 in English. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could the witness -- it's probably a relatively short statement, before he is asked questions about part could he be allowed to read the whole since it is apparent that General Tolimir wants to ask him questions about this document. This is a -- well, I won't say anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, please read whatever you want to familiarise yourself -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just want to ask him questions about a relevant paragraph, but I don't object him to reading if we're going to waste time. However, I wanted to ask him questions only about a relevant paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were referring to two paragraphs, the first one of it starts with the words: "As we made our way through the direction ..." and so on, and the next paragraph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since you are reading the English version I wanted to show exactly what you quoted and I quote the relevant paragraph. It's paragraph 3 in the Serbian language, line 4: "From there, we headed towards Pobudjanska-Kamenica where we met with part of the first group. But the Chetniks surrounded us there and opened fire on us, killing over 300 people and wounding a large number. We were in disarray as both soldiers and civilians fled wherever they could while the wounded were left behind on the path."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question based on this quote: As an investigator, did you know about this piece of information that the OTP received in July of 1996? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't specifically remember reading this document. I have certainly read a similar account, and I have probably read this document. It -- it is familiar to me that parts of the column were attacked and that individuals were killed. I accept that the Tribunal was aware of that sort of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he is to allowed the whole document I think he would be able to provide a better answer. But since he has only read part of, he could only provide part of answer. And I know this document very well, so I know that it's not -- it's not just -- irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tolimir knows this document as well and should conduct his examination as he wants, and we will give way to that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to say that the questions put by Mr. McCloskey could be left for his re-examination. But he should not suggest Mr. Tolimir want to do during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should not go on in this way. I would like to invite Mr. Tolimir to continue his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I may speak just briefly, Your Honour. This is normal discussion, believe me. The question was: Do you remember the document. The document is of four or five pages. It could be the most memorable part of the document is the last page that's not been shown to the witness. So to get a fair answer out of the witness to do you remember the document, he should be able to see the whole document. It's a smart -- I don't intend to -- to determine what questions he asks. But when he asks do you remember the document to probably a four- or five-page document, that refers to the entire document, and so he, in my view, should be able to view the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the witness provided Mr. Tolimir with an answer to that question. Go ahead Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't ask whether he remembered but whether this document was written before he started investigating the events and before they became known to the OTP, and he replied I might have read it. But I don't want to waste any time. It's just a relevant piece of information that this particular witness saw 300 killed and many more wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where these people were buried? Yes, that would be my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why the Prosecution did not investigate information that was familiar to it? Where they would have needed less money and fewer teams when they went to investigate graves.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe it's fair to say the Prosecution did not investigate. Clearly we would take statements from individuals, we would conduct inquiries, conduct investigations. In this instance, and I would need to check, I don't believe that we located those bodies. But, remember, we were examining, as part of an exhumation project, mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. My question is: Do you perhaps know in which mass grave these surface remains were later buried, the remains that this witness talks about, these 300 people killed and many more wounded? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not part of that process, but I would suggest, from what I know, that those remains have been collected by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and have been or are being examined for DNA and matched to Srebrenica victims or whomever. The answer to the question is that those individuals on the surface were - I hope - collected by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and the families reunited with those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. During today's examination-in-chief, you said that you were present when international pathologists and anthropologist handed over to the Bosnian side the remaining graves. Were surface remains - the surface remains that you're talking about now - were they also handed over to them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be specific, the remains weren't handed over to the Bosnian commission. Responsibility for the named mass graves was handed to the Bosnian commission, and, in fact, it wasn't anthropologists or archaeologists, it was the OTP, produced a document, I wrote it, which said: You are hereby responsible hereafter for the exhumation of these identified mass graves and the exhumation and examination of other mass graves that you may find connected to the Srebrenica case. I also, in a separate process handed bodies over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, and the responsibility for the examination of surface remains, I can't comment on whether that was a responsibility handed to the Bosnians by the OTP. I was involved in the mass grave process and not the collection of surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16 of today's transcript, in line 5, you said that the International Court - and you said the International Court - handed over, that is, made a decision for the continuing work and the exhumations be left to the Bosnian government. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I don't think I said "International Court." But the responsibility for the continuing exhumation of the mass graves was handed to the Bosnian authorities by the OTP, by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I suppose by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I owe a correction. It was page 10, line 5. Thank you for your answer. My question is: Could you please tell us now who made the decision that this responsibility for the exhumations be transferred to the national team of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the international teams?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Ultimately by the Prosecutor, the Chief Prosecutor for the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia; I believe at that stage, Madam Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just for clarity of the record, on page 10, line 5, the witness is recorded to having said: "Your Honours, prior to the hand-over, the ICTY held responsibility for the exhumation of all the Srebrenica mass-related graves," I think mass graves, related, "and execution points and were conducting a programme," and so on and so on. He was referring to the ICTY, in particular. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. In light of this, I would like to ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it the International Court that had jurisdiction until now, that is the ICTY, or was it the OTP that decided to transfer responsibility from the international courts to the national courts in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's difficult to answer in that way. The OTP is an organ of the ICTY, is part of the ICTY. Ultimately the decision was made by the ICTY that we not continue with the exhumation process, that it be handed over to the Bosnian authorities and to the International Commission for Missing Persons. So ultimately the decision was an ICTY one. I can't now recall whether that was driven by the OTP, whether it was a decision made in the UN. I can't recall the process of why that decision was made, only that I was tasked with drawing up the agreement that said, These graves and these sites are now your responsibility, and we would like to monitor that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you wrote the agreement whereby the responsibility was transferred to BH teams, and you said a moment ago that this decision was made by Madam Del Ponte, in order for us to know exactly who made the decision, is there a written decision on the transfer of responsibility from the ICTY to the -- BH? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a document which exists. I can't recall who signed it, but it's an agreement for that hand-over. Perhaps the chief of investigations signed it. Perhaps it was signed by Madam Del Ponte; I can't recall. It exists, and it's available, I assume, within the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. What I'd like to know is if the document states based on whose decision the OTP transferred responsibility onto the BH authorities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd have to check the document. I didn't take that decision. I don't believe the chief of investigations took that decision. Ultimately, a decision of that nature would have been approved and taken by the Prosecutor, the Chief Prosecutor. We need to check the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, when you have an opportunity to do so, during your testimony, if you could check and see what the document states on this score. This is my next question. Do you know -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning is, of course, no longer employed, and the Court -- we can try to always go into the archives of Ms. Del Ponte to determine if there -- such a document exists and perhaps request New York's permission to get it. We'll look. So -- but, of course, Mr. Manning is not in a position to do that. But we can endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We thought that this could be found among the papers which make up Mr. Manning's statements and reports. At any rate, do you know Jean-Rene Ruez? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if he worked as your predecessor or did you work for the OTP of this Tribunal at the same time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez was my direct supervisor when I arrived at the Tribunal. I worked for him for a number of years. He left the Tribunal and I then worked for another team leader. I worked for Mr. Ruez and with Mr. Ruez for three, three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now show 1D100 in e-court, page 7, lines 8 through 18. This is from the Krstic case. Before I put my question, I ought to tell you that Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez testified in the case against Mr. Krstic and stated as follows. I quote -- and I would also circle the village of Bare. It's been taken off my screen and I wasn't able to continue reading. So let's see what he said in lines 8 through 17 in that particular case and before that Trial Chamber. So I'm quoting from line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now we need the English version. Which page, which line? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, that's 595, line 8 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In e-court that is page 7. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, once again. It was not heard by the interpreters and the recorder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English translation, that is page 7 in e-court. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wish to thank Mr. Registrar. Let's see what Mr. Ruez said in his testimony of this case: "This area has been processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who were operating in that area in 1996, totally disconnected from our activities. They were collecting surface remains. But it's important to note that 600 bodies have been collected in that area. These are bodies of victims killed in combat, in ambushes, in shelling, and possibly also in other circumstances which are impossible to sort out between -- I mean, for us, at least, between combat and other situations." Based on what I've just read out, this is my question: Were you aware of this extent of Mr. Ruez's testimony, of what he is talking about here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was aware that surface remains had been collected. From my memory, I didn't realise it was the Fins. I was not involved in that process. It was two years before I started. I was generally aware of it but it was not part of my investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the record, I note that this document is not in the list of potential exhibits to be used with this witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a reference to a witness who testified in this case, but we -- in the future, we will notify you of this too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the purpose of these lists, to -- to enable the other party and the Chamber to prepare. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you know what became of these 600 surface remains who were a result of combat? Where were they ultimately buried and where were their bodies and artefacts exhumed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a misstatement of what Mr. Ruez said. He is leaving out part of it, the key part of it, in my view. He should be not -- he shouldn't make a misstatement like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Ruez, in this document, said: "For us, at least, it was not possible to -- it was impossible to sort out between combat and other situations." And now you are only referring to combat. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, this is my question: Do you know where these surface remains are buried, in what grave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, remembering that I wasn't involved in this process, I can say that the surface remains collected were stored for many years in Tuzla in salt mines, in the tunnels that previously were used as salt mines. I saw many of those body-bags and collections of bodies. They were not reburied in that process. They were examined and eventually returned to the families, those that could be, and then buried in individual graves, I assume. The -- to my knowledge, the bodies collected as surface remains were stored in Tuzla by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Since they were taken to Tuzla from the location they were found at, at Bare, can you tell us, were they listed in your reports as missing, or -- or those executed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The bodies referred to by Mr. Ruez were not counted in my reports, and I have limited knowledge about what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if DNA analysis was made for any of the bodies recovered at the location in Bare we've just referred to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know that specifically, but the Podrinje Identification Project and ICMP intend to DNA register every human remain that was located right across Bosnia. So, yes, they would be examined. They may already have been; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Since you don't know but you say that it is possible that they were registered, is there a list of these 600 individuals with their first and last names in the cases where they were identified? And were all DNA identifications entered into the lists drawn up by anthropologists and matched against the lists of those who had gone missing or were killed in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know in relation to the bodies referred to by Mr. Ruez, but ICMP and the Bosnian commission are examining all the remains, and those identified as coming from Srebrenica or elsewhere are included on their list of identified bodies from the Bosnian conflict. I can't answer your questions in relation to these bodies because I wasn't involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to see the report from the Finnish experts who worked on this? And, to your knowledge, can such a report be found in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't recall reading it. I may have done. We're talking 12 years or more. I don't recall, but I may have read it. It may be in the possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further need of this document. I have just one last question related to this issue. Is it possible that these individuals, too, once they were identified, were entered on the list of those who had gone missing in relation to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P170. I apologise if this document was not notified in advance. This is Dusan Janc's report from 2010, page 43, where he, too, refers to surface remains. That's page 43 in English and 60 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is not in your list. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President. Let me use this opportunity before the document appears, the questions related to this document arose during the OTP's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Thank you, Mr. President, for your understanding. Can we look at paragraph 2 of the document in Serbian, and it is the corresponding paragraph 2 in English. It reads, and I quote, this is the report by Mr. Janc: "The analysis establishes that 688 Srebrenica-related individuals in total have currently been identified from 961 surface remains cases. This figure consists of 653 identified persons on the February 2010 ICMP update together with 35 identified persons on the surface remains data only (see surface remains portion of confidential Annex D). The 653 individuals from the ICMP update were determined to be surface remains based on their case IDs, which correspond to the case IDs found in the surface remains data (ERN X018-9698-X018-9712)." Let's look at footnote 3 that he refers to. It says: "35 identified persons included in the surface data cannot be found on the March 2009 ICMP update. In addition, three of the identified persons included in the surface remains data appear to have gone missing in 1993," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Can you tell us, were there cases in the documents that you looked at and which you received from the Bosnian side and other bodies and commissions working on the recovery of victims that individuals from 1993 had been included this those lists?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. Again, I'd have to check, but I don't recall being provided with data which related to 1993. I would have requested data from Srebrenica from 1995. So, no, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now. And we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Hello, Witness. We will resume. We were looking at the portion of Mr. Janc's report where he numbered the surface remains. My question is this: Were all these surface remains found by the individuals who found them on the same spot where they were lying all the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't answer that question. I wasn't involved in the collection of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the last paragraph on page 11 in Serbian which says -- or can we have the previous page back, please. My mistake. Can we have the page we were on before back on our screens? And in English too. Thank you. It's page 60 in Serbian and 43 in English. I'm reading from the last paragraph: "The locations where Srebrenica-related surface remains have been collected are consistent with the locations through which the Muslim column leaving from Susnjari ... was passing?" And then he goes on to list the areas: "Pobudje, (Bratunac-Konjevic Polje); next, Baljkovica (Zvornik); next Snagovo, also close to Zvornik; and other locations, other areas outside the above-mentioned areas but still relatively close to them?" This is my question: Were these surface remains counted together with those individuals who were recovered from the mass graves when it came to DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, not in my report, or my reports. I've not read Mr. Janc's report. He may have done so, I did not. I did not count the surface remains, except, from memory, the individuals at Kozluk which we were discussing earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the remains referred to by Dusan Janc were not discovered at the time when you were involved in investigations and that it was only when he was producing this analysis in 2010 that these remains were referred to? Thank you. Yes, the year was 2010, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In fact, in my report from the ICMP data, I referred to collections of surface remains. I think I even indicated the areas and the abbreviations for those surface remains, but I did not count those surface remains and I did not include them in the report. This report I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. All these missing persons listed in the records of the commission and the international committee which dealt with the lists and identification, were they all contained in your reports at the time when you appeared as a witness in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My initial reports dealt with the number of victims within the mass graves, and that was an anthropological assessment. My 2007 report dealt with the bodies from those mass graves which had been identified via DNA. I did not include other lists. I included the numbers of Srebrenica-identified individuals who were located in Srebrenica-related mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of this answer, this is my next question: You were the chief investigator of the ICTY in the Srebrenica-related cases; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. I was one of the senior investigators. There was a team leader above me, and I was a member of the team, and specifically I was involved in the co-ordination of the exhumation investigation areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who chose the title of your operation, i.e., Casper? Why was this particular name chosen, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if there was such a name used at the time when you were the senior member of the investigations team?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The team was known as Casper. I don't know why it was called Casper. It was referred to as Team 6 in those days, or the Casper Team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell us briefly what were the duties you performed as an OTP investigator in searching for potential witnesses or perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In addition to the exhumations responsibilities, I was a general investigator. I would seek to identify witnesses, take statements from them, examine crime scenes, show photographs to witnesses. I was involved in the interview of suspects. I was involved in search warrants, looking for evidence. General investigative duties, including the interview of witnesses and suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Manning, tell us, the majority of the reports you produced for the OTP, do they have to do with forensic evidence as you stated in the Popovic case at transcript page 18905, lines 13 through 22? Where you state, and I'm quoting you. You say that you helped experts who were preparing for their work. You asked what it involved, and your answer was: "In certain occasions, I would accompany experts on field trips to various grave-sites or I would attend exhumations at -- of mass graves. I would give them information that was available to the OTP out in the field or in the morgue. Essentially, I had access to all the information we had in various files. The exhumations started in 1996 and went on until 2001. Thus, I had an overview of available information of all the locations and other relevant information." Based on what you stated in the Popovic case, at page 18905, tell us this: When you say that you provided experts with various information, can you tell us specifically what the information was about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to have that part of the testimony of the witness on the screen. This is 65 ter 06765. That is the public version. Page 18905.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, to give -- to give you an example, in relation to Dr. Anthony Brown, I provided Dr. Brown access to the grave-sites. He collected soil samples and pollen samples and he used that in his investigations. I would have also provided him with documentation related to the exhumation, when it occurred, who -- the expert reports that he would need to make his report. I did a similar thing with Professor Wright when it came that he had left the Tribunal and needed to write his reports. He would ask me for the information, the copies of documents, the copies of photographs, CDs, et cetera, which allowed him to write his report. He produced the reports, and I put those reports into evidence. I did that with all the experts. For instance, Suzi Maljaars, Dr. Maljaars, from the Netherlands forensic institute, I provided her with the blindfolds and cloth ligatures, and she provided me with the report which I had translated and then I examined that report. So that sort of assistance was what I provided to the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Based what you said, I would like to ask this: Did you tell the experts only about your information of forensic nature, or did you also provide them with information about the events in Srebrenica 95 and tell them the position of the OTP on what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I think, sir, you [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] may be suggesting that I could influence the experts. That's not the case. I provided them with the information. They produced their reports based on that information. If they were to ask me information in relation to where Srebrenica was or where the graves were, factual information, I would provide it. I didn't provide them with the OTP's view of what the evidence should be. I provided them with the information for which they then produced their independent reports to the Tribunal, which they later, in several trials, discussed and presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So that I can ask my next question, please tell me what your powers were in relation to the anthropologists and the pathologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. They were employed as experts by the Office of the Prosecutor. I worked with them. They were -- say, the chief archaeologist was in charge of the exhumation project from an archaeological point of view. I was in charge of the investigation point of view. I would be treated as an equal. But he would look after his people. Same with the mortuary; the chief pathologist was in charge of the mortuary, and then I would assist him and his team with whatever they needed. And if there was a dispute, and there sometimes was, the matter would be raised with the OTP and it would be decided by the OTP. And by "dispute" I mean if we indicated that we wanted this grave done because of some scheduling and they wanted to do another grave because of their interests, that sort of matter, if it couldn't be sorted out would be referred to the Tribunal. But I was not their supervisors, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one thing on the record. Page 73, line 25, it is written here: "I think, sir, I may be suggesting" -- I have to wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "I think, sir, I may be suggesting that I could influence the experts." I understood you in a different way. I heard you saying: "I think sir, you may be suggesting that I could influence the experts."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, I don't want to forget it. You used the document 1D100. This is the testimony of Mr. Ruez in the Krstic trial. This is now listed as the last document in your list of exhibits to be used with this witness. Are you tendering this part of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender it as an exhibit, if possible, and then I would ask some questions -- I would ask some further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In relation to that exhibit, I -- otherwise, I would ask you if you are tendering only that page you have shown to the witness or the, altogether, I think nine or ten pages of that transcript? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to tender all ten pages of the transcript, since it's difficult to understand that single paragraph without the rest of it, especially without what's on the previous pages. We believe that this will not be too many pages and it's clear from the transcript which page was used and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D166. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Please tell me who managed or co-ordinated the work of the anthropologist and pathologist; that is, who was in charge of the organisation of the work at the time when you were engaged in this matters?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a exhumations team which was normally headed by a chief archaeologist. He would then have a team of up to 40 individuals working for him in the field. He would control those people. At the mortuary, there was a chief pathologist who was in charge of the mortuary, and he would control those people and they would work to him. And he would produce a report detailing the work. The chief archaeologist would produce a report detailing the work of his team. I acted as a co-ordinator of those efforts and represented the interests of the OTP and the investigation across those two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell me why, then, it was that when the anthropologist presented their report they said, Ask such and such an investigator about this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, no, the chief anthropologist or pathologist, for instance, Dr. Clark would say to me from his base in Scotland, Could you provide me with the following information, could you provide me with the photographs from body 200, et cetera, et cetera, and I would provide that material to him to assist him in producing his reports. I was a conduit between the OTP and the experts, and I was also able to provide them with information related to, say, previous expert reports or previous exhumations in which they were not involved. So Professor Wright might say to me, I wasn't involved in X exhumation, X exhumation, can you tell me when that happened and provide me photographs. That was the nature of my assistance to them, as well as taking them into the field, when necessary, such as Professor Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Bearing in mind what you said, please tell me whether your task or job also included telling these teams where surface graves were found or located and to tell them about the fact that the OTP had registered them as such graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The OTP exhumations team were not examining surface remains. I'm sorry, you'll have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to guess, so please tell me who examined surface remains then?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As I've indicated, surface remains were generally collected by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, ICMP, and, as you pointed out, a Finnish commission. We were exhuming mass graves that I have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a report that was compiled by the Swedish commission, and did you have the reports by the Bosnian commission that was headed by Amir Masovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In relation to what specifically? Surface remains?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure I've read those reports. I dealt with Mr. Masovic. I requested information in relation to exhumations. I don't specifically recall that, and I didn't incorporate that material into my reports, which were related to the Srebrenica mass graves, not the surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when, as you said, you handed matters over to the federal government and to the federal commissions, did you know at the time what function Amir Masovic held during the war, whether he had been a member of the BH army, whether he was a member of the exchange commission, and might that have had any influence on the job that he was later doing, the responsibilities that you handed over to him?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I am aware that Mr. Masovic was involved in the transfer of bodies during the war, that had no impact on the decision to hand over the bodies -- sorry, the responsibility for the mass graves to the Bosnian commission. That responsibility was handed to the commission, not to Mr. Masovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was Mr. Masovic working in that federal commission to which you entrusted the work that had been done by the international commissions and international bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And you - and it was you who decided to hand matters over - did you investigate the role of Mr. Masovic during 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, if possible, let's look at the transcript, 1946 from the Popovic case, and I will quote what you said: "I was involved" -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 0675. Once again, this is 65 ter 0675. It's on the screen. Please indicate which page you want to see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted 1904, lines 2 to 7, from the Popovic case. I might have misspoken; I apologise. I would like to quote that to the witness. Thank you. And I quote what the witness said on that page in lines 2 to 7. The witness said, I quote: "I was involved" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen, Mr. Tolimir. I think it can't be the right page. 1904. We have now 18905 on the screen. Could you please check again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like 1904, lines 2 to 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now 18904. Do you mean that page, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted 1904. Page 1904.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That can't be -- this can't be the right page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I might have written down the wrong reference. I would like to read what the witness said and then maybe based on that, we will later find the page and have the correct reference. I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would be happy if that could be enlarged. Please, continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I was involved in an operation in which weapons were seized from the Bratunac and other brigades. These weapons were then tested and the cartridges were examined by the ATF. At that time, these weapons were returned to the relevant units. In that case, we did not examine the weapons forensically but we examined the casings which had been fired from those weapons. It's probably the same thing." And after you were presented with the statement that you had given in the Blagojevic cases where you said that the results of the tests were wrong, as you said, negative, in lines 21 to 25 you said, and I quote: "According to my information, the firing of bullets for testing resulted in hundreds of casings. These were examined and they were negative; that is, they were unreliable. But I wasn't involved in the final stages of this process. However, I agree that the results were negative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't have the right page on the screen. Again, please check the page number. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will check immediately about the page number and give you the correct reference. Some numbers might have been permutated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Manning never said wrong or unreliable in that context, but I'm sure he will remember the subject matter and can answer questions on it without a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure he can, but we want to have the right page on the screen. But, first, I would invite Mr. Tolimir to put his question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you say that the results were negative after bullets were fired from the weapon that had been seized from the Bratunac and other brigades? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what was the goal of this forensic examination? Why were bullets fired or rounds fired from these seized weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spoke before about the shell cases which had been collected from the mass graves. We seized a significant number of weapons. We took those to a military base, an American military base. I was in charge of the operation to fire two rounds from each weapon that could be fired. We collected the shell case, the two shell cases that we produced, and they were then conveyed to the ATF, American Alcohol, Tobacco, and Fire-Arms Agency, to compare to the shell cases which we had previously found in the mass graves. The process was designed to see if any of those weapons that we seized were the same as the weapons that had fired the shell cases, which had been found in the mass graves. To my knowledge, that was negative, but the OTP and the investigations team could update you as to what happened thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The proper transcript page for that, I believe we found is 19094, where he is speaking of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, for the reference, for the page reference. I would now like to look at this exhibit, 1D595, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not on the list of your documents to be used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is just a part of what he said, what Mr. Manning said during his previous testimony. I apologise that we didn't put it on the list. We didn't know that we would need to get to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Manning to look at the part where it says, clearly, it says: "The results of the examination show that none of these cartridge cases previously submitted under this laboratory number and listed as submissions 1 through 7." My question is: During your investigation, did you ever obtain the weapons which you used to fire the rounds that were sent to investigation -- during your examination of the mass graves, did you ever obtain those weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you mean did we locate the weapons that had fired the bullets and the shell cases located within the mass graves, not to my knowledge, no, we did not. But, again, OTP could update that. But not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please tell me why this was sent to the bureau for alcohol, tobacco and fire-arms? Were there any indications beforehand about anything or was this sent based on the personal assessment of the investigator involved? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sir, if you are referring to this document, I had left the Tribunal when this process was undertaken, so I can't answer in relation to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind what you said, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to admit document 1D591, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it just this page or is it a voluminous report? I don't know about that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a one-page report. It is a one-page report, as far as I know. And 1D591 is, indeed, on the list that I sent. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We had earlier another number. Yes, on your list, you have 1D591. But, on the screen, we have 1D595. Perhaps it was a typo in your list; I don't know. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this particular document, as far as I know, does reflect the subject -- same subject matter that the witness has talked about. I think the results just came in formally after he'd left. So this is connected to this material, and we have no objection to it going into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a small clarification. 1D591 is, indeed, the document that we see on the screen. I'm looking at the version which I can see in e-court and what we have on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we received a wrong translation or whatever. But now it's clarified and this document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D591 shall be assigned Exhibit D167. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this concludes the hearing of today. We have to adjourn. And we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Please be reminded that you are not allowed to communicate with either party about the content of your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
